actions.name: Review recent hospitalization/illness record
actions.result: Treated for pneumonia/chest infection 5 weeks ago by primary care; course of oral antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate x7 days), no hospitalization, with symptom resolution. Documented as 'community-acquired pneumonia, right lower lobe, resolved' per PCP note. Chest X-ray at the time showed a right lower lobe infiltrate.

actions.name: Review weight trend in chart
actions.result: Weight 68.0 kg three months ago; 66.2 kg six weeks ago; 64.0 kg today. Steady downward trend across all three recorded points.

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg, 1 tablet PO four times daily with meals and at bedtime; patient reports tablets sometimes stick in throat before swallowing.

actions.name: Observed trial swallow: thin liquid (water), camera view
actions.result: Patient swallows 5 mL water on camera. Voice sounds wet/gurgly immediately after swallow. Delayed cough response approximately 8-10 seconds after the swallow. No overt choking.

actions.name: Observed trial swallow: thicker consistency (yogurt via spoon)
actions.result: Patient swallows one spoonful of yogurt. No wet vocal quality noted after this trial. No immediate or delayed cough observed over 1 minute of monitoring.

actions.name: Cervical auscultation during swallow (caregiver-assisted, phone/stethoscope if available)
actions.result: Caregiver reports no stethoscope available at home; cervical auscultation could not be performed this visit.

actions.name: Perceptual voice screening (sustained /ah/, max phonation time)
actions.result: Sustained /ah/ produced for 6 seconds (reduced; expected >15-20 sec for age). Voice quality: breathy, monotone, reduced loudness (hypophonic). Pitch and loudness variability markedly reduced.

actions.name: Oral mechanism exam via camera (lips, tongue, jaw, velum)
actions.result: Facial masking noted, reduced spontaneous blink rate. Lip seal adequate at rest but reduced lip rounding/retraction range. Tongue protrusion and lateralization present but slowed with reduced range. Palate elevates symmetrically on 'ah'. No overt facial asymmetry.

actions.name: Diadochokinetic rate (repeat 'puh-tuh-kuh')
actions.result: Slow and effortful; rate reduced compared to age norms, with some imprecision on sequential motion rate; consistent with hypokinetic dysarthria pattern.

actions.name: Functional communication/participation screening (interview-based)
actions.result: Patient reports stopping attendance at weekly community gathering over past 2 months because others ask him to repeat himself; reports frustration and embarrassment but denies feeling depressed.

actions.name: Review prior neurology note on Parkinson disease staging
actions.result: Neurology note from 6 months ago: Parkinson disease, Hoehn and Yahr stage 3, moderate bilateral bradykinesia and rigidity, mild postural instability. No prior formal speech or swallow referral on file.

actions.name: Caregiver-reported mealtime duration and behaviors
actions.result: Wife reports meals now take over 60 minutes (previously about 25-30 minutes), with frequent coughing on tea and water at most meals and patient needing to re-swallow pills multiple times.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he does not choke and has no swallowing difficulty.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Primary care note documents a recent right lower lobe pneumonia requiring antibiotic treatment, and chest X-ray confirmed a right lower lobe infiltrate; this recent pulmonary event in a patient with Parkinson disease and caregiver-reported coughing on liquids is inconsistent with his report of no swallowing problems.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients, especially those with Parkinson disease, often have reduced laryngeal sensation and may genuinely be unaware of aspiration; clinicians must weigh caregiver report and medical record evidence over self-report alone, and silent aspiration should be considered even when the patient denies symptoms.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient suggests the referral for speech-language evaluation only came up casually after his pneumonia and he didn't feel it was urgent.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Neurology note from 6 months prior already documented 'speech noted to be soft but not formally assessed' with no referral made at that time, and the PCP note from 5 weeks ago explicitly recommended SLP follow-up, indicating a documented pattern of noted concerns and delayed action over time rather than a single casual mention.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Review of longitudinal records can reveal that warning signs (such as soft speech) were noted earlier but not acted upon; this highlights the importance of timely referral when hypophonia or swallowing concerns are first observed in progressive neurological disease.

objectives.text: Elicit a swallowing history from both patient and caregiver, recognizing discrepancies between patient self-report and caregiver-observed signs of dysphagia.
Identify clinical signs of aspiration risk during observed oral intake trials, including delayed cough and wet vocal quality.
Recognize red flags warranting urgent instrumental swallow evaluation, including unintentional weight loss and recent aspiration pneumonia.
Assess hypokinetic dysarthria and hypophonia associated with Parkinson disease through perceptual voice and oral motor screening.
Identify the patient-record mismatch regarding awareness/reporting of swallowing difficulty and discuss how silent aspiration can occur in Parkinson disease.

Formulate an appropriate, in-scope plan including referral for instrumental swallow study (e.g., videofluoroscopic swallow study), interim compensatory strategies, and recommendation of LSVT LOUD for voice treatment, respecting patient autonomy and dignity.

profile.summary: A 73-year-old man with 8-year history of Parkinson disease presents for telehealth swallow and communication evaluation after a recent aspiration pneumonia, with caregiver-reported coughing on liquids, prolonged meal times, and unintentional weight loss, despite the patient denying any swallowing difficulty. The case teaches recognition of silent aspiration risk, hypokinetic dysarthria/hypophonia, and appropriate in-scope referral for instrumental swallow evaluation and LSVT LOUD, while modeling respectful management of a proud patient who dislikes being discussed in the third person.
profile.title: Silent Aspiration Risk and Hypophonia in a Man with Parkinson Disease Who Denies Swallowing Difficulty
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home at the dining table with his wife, suburban Chicago

answerKey.primaryProblem: Oropharyngeal dysphagia with aspiration risk and hypokinetic dysarthria/hypophonia secondary to Parkinson disease
differential: Parkinson disease-related oropharyngeal dysphagia with silent aspiration
Hypokinetic dysarthria with hypophonia secondary to Parkinson disease
Medication (carbidopa-levodopa) pill dysphagia contributing to intake difficulty
Reflux-related or structural esophageal dysphagia (less likely given denial of reflux symptoms, exam pattern favors oropharyngeal/neurogenic cause)
Unintentional weight loss from reduced oral intake secondary to dysphagia versus decreased appetite alone
keyFindings: Caregiver-reported coughing on tea and water at most meals; meals now take over an hour
4 kg (5.9%) unintentional weight loss over 3 months
Recent aspiration-related pneumonia 5 weeks ago per primary care documentation and chest X-ray
Wet vocal quality and delayed cough (8-10 seconds) after observed thin liquid trial on camera
No wet voice or cough noted with thicker (yogurt) consistency trial
Patient denies any swallowing difficulty despite objective and caregiver evidence of aspiration risk
Carbidopa-levodopa tablets reported to stick in throat at mealtimes
Reduced maximum phonation time (6 seconds), breathy/monotone/hypophonic voice
Reduced diadochokinetic rate and oral motor range consistent with hypokinetic dysarthria
Social withdrawal from valued weekly community gathering due to communication breakdown
plan: Recommend referral for an instrumental swallow evaluation (videofluoroscopic swallow study, VFSS) given red flags: recent aspiration pneumonia, significant unintentional weight loss, wet voice and delayed cough on thin liquids

Recommend interim compensatory strategies pending instrumental study: trial of nectar-thick or thickened liquids for high-risk thin liquids (tea, water), chin-tuck posture during swallows, smaller bites/sips, remaining upright for 30 minutes post-meal

Discuss medication administration strategy with patient and prescribing provider: consider alternative pill-taking strategy (e.g., with puree or thickened liquid) or formulation review if tablets continue to stick, in coordination with neurology/pharmacy
Recommend and discuss initiating LSVT LOUD voice treatment to address hypophonia and improve functional communication participation
Refer back to primary care/neurology with findings; communicate aspiration risk and weight loss findings given overlap with medical management

Address patient's stated goal (returning to community gathering) by framing voice treatment and swallowing strategies in terms of his functional priorities, respecting his autonomy and avoiding paternalistic framing
Schedule follow-up SLP visit to review instrumental study results and finalize treatment plan
redFlags: Unintentional weight loss of 5.9% body weight over 3 months
Wet vocal quality and delayed cough with thin liquids on observed trial, suggesting possible silent aspiration
Patient's denial of symptoms despite objective and caregiver evidence, raising concern for reduced laryngeal sensation and risk of continued silent aspiration without intervention
educationPoints: Patients with Parkinson disease may have reduced laryngeal sensation and can silently aspirate without overt coughing or choking, so self-report alone is insufficient for ruling out dysphagia
Wet vocal quality and delayed cough after swallowing are clinical indicators warranting further instrumental evaluation, not a diagnosis of aspiration itself

Hypophonia and monotone speech in Parkinson disease (hypokinetic dysarthria) can significantly impact social participation and quality of life, and is a distinct but related treatment target from swallowing
LSVT LOUD is an evidence-based, intensive voice treatment specifically designed for individuals with Parkinson disease to improve vocal loudness and intelligibility

Respecting patient autonomy and addressing the patient directly, especially when caregivers are present, is essential for building trust and encouraging adherence, particularly in patients who value independence and dislike being discussed in the third person
Unintentional weight loss combined with recent aspiration pneumonia are objective red flags that should prompt referral for instrumental swallow assessment regardless of patient-reported symptoms
